source.title: Shortcut learning in deep neural networks
source.authors: Robert Geirhos; J. Jacobsen; Claudio Michaelis; R. Zemel; Wieland Brendel; M. Bethge; Felix Wichmann

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including the appendix with toy experiment details.
record.tranche_reason: This perspective discusses generalization and reports a toy experiment about out-of-distribution location shifts. That experiment does not test the claim's same-distribution generalization versions; the text explicitly distinguishes i.i.d. from out-of-distribution testing.
record.gate_note: The toy experiment compares a fully connected network and a convolutional network on randomly positioned shapes. Its test set changes the training location distribution, so the result is out-of-distribution and does not test the mapped claim versions. The paper also summarizes cited studies; those are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The original toy experiment tests V3 in a new image setting: under a location distribution shift, the convolutional network achieves lower held-out error than the fully connected network trained with the same optimizer and budget. V3 does not explicitly restrict its comparison to i.i.d. tests; the shift qualifies the setting rather than excluding the result.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: shortcut learning can produce strong i.i.d. performance while failing under changed testing conditions, so i.i.d. performance alone cannot distinguish intended from shortcut solutions. The authors recommend careful interpretation, out-of-distribution testing, and investigation of architectural, data, loss and optimization biases.
record.recipe_differences: A perspective article with a small synthetic toy experiment on out-of-distribution location shifts; it does not reproduce the claim's same-distribution experiments or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture changes the toy experiment's outcome under randomized test locations: the fully connected network reaches approximately chance-level test accuracy, while the convolutional network reaches 100% on train and test.
record.problems: The only original quantitative experiment is a synthetic toy task and tests an out-of-distribution location shift. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for interpolation.

Comparisons on the named natural-image benchmarks; isolated contributions of local connectivity versus weight sharing and pooling; sparse fully connected networks and initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer performance and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Effects of dropout, training-set size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The architecture comparison supports V3 only in this synthetic distribution-shift setting. It does not isolate local connectivity as the cause: the convolutional architecture also includes weight sharing and global average pooling. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Same-distribution image test error for convolutional versus fully connected networks, and the role of local connectivity.
Held-out performance across adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers and tuning conditions.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across training-set sizes and regularization conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to same-distribution train-test gaps.
Effect of removing memorized training examples on test accuracy.
